introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Time allowed: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklet are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (One hour): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (30 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (1 hour): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown: State and explain how the electrical resistance of each of the following will be affected by an increase in temperature; pure semiconductor
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The resistance of a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor decreases as the temperature rises.**

At low temperature almost all the valence electrons are bound in covalent bonds, so very few charge carriers are available. When the temperature rises, more electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross the (small) energy gap into the conduction band, each leaving a hole in the valence band. The number of free charge carriers per unit volume ($n$ electrons and $n$ holes) increases rapidly, roughly exponentially with temperature. Since the current is $I = nAve$, the increase in the number of carriers far outweighs the small increase in lattice vibrations, so the **resistivity falls** and the resistance decreases. (A semiconductor therefore has a **negative temperature coefficient of resistance**; this is the principle of the thermistor.)

questions.enonce_markdown: pure metal wire *[4 marks for question 2]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The resistance of a pure metal wire increases as the temperature rises.**

A metal already contains a very large number of free electrons, and this number is practically unchanged by heating. When the temperature rises, the positive ions of the lattice vibrate with larger amplitudes, so the conduction electrons collide more often with them. The mean time between collisions decreases, so for the same applied p.d. the drift velocity (and hence the current) is smaller. The resistivity $\rho$ increases, and with it the resistance $R = \rho l / A$. For a limited temperature range the relation is $R_\theta = R_0(1 + \alpha\theta)$ with $\alpha > 0$: a **positive temperature coefficient of resistance**.
